claims.claim: Without configuration, loggers pass WARNING and above, and the last-resort handler prints only the message; LoggerAdapter adds context; logger.exception includes the traceback.
claims.source: Run in Python 3.11 in this repository.

concept_html:
print writes text to standard output, with no level, no source and no context. In a scheduled job, that text lands in a driver log that nobody searches until something breaks.

Python's standard logging module fixes all three problems.

One logger per module. log = logging.getLogger(__name__) names the logger after the module, such as pipelines.silver. Every line then says where it came from.

Levels. DEBUG for detail while developing, INFO for normal milestones, WARNING for something odd that did not stop the run, ERROR for a failure, CRITICAL for a failure that stops everything. Loggers pass WARNING and above by default, so log.info(...) prints nothing until you configure a level.

Context on every line. Include the identifiers you will search for later: run_id, tracker_id, wave_id, layer. A LoggerAdapter attaches them once, and a format string prints them:

base = logging.getLogger(__name__)
log = logging.LoggerAdapter(base, {"run_id": run_id, "wave_id": wave_id})
log.info("merged rows=%d", n)
# INFO pipelines.silver run_id=7f3c wave_id=W14 merged rows=1832

Three more rules:

  • Pass values as arguments, log.info("rows=%d", n), not pre-built f-strings. The logger formats them only when the line is actually emitted.
  • Inside except, call log.exception("..."). It logs at ERROR and appends the full traceback.
  • Configure handlers and formats once, in the entry point, never inside library functions.

Logs are for people reading one run. Metrics you want to compare across runs, such as row counts and statuses, also go to the run log table (lesson A7-L2).

lines: import logging
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
def merge_wave(df: DataFrame, run_id: str, wave_id: str) -> int:
"""MERGE one wave, logging with run and wave context. Re-raises on failure."""
log = logging.LoggerAdapter(logger, {"run_id": run_id, "wave_id": wave_id})
log.info("merge started")
try:
rows = do_merge(df)
except Exception:
log.exception("merge failed")
raise
if rows == 0:
log.warning("merge wrote 0 rows")
else:
log.info("merge finished rows=%d", rows)
return rows

import io
import logging
_stream = io.StringIO()
_handler = logging.StreamHandler(_stream)
_handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(levelname)s run_id=%(run_id)s wave_id=%(wave_id)s %(message)s"))
_base = logging.getLogger("pipelines.silver")
_base.handlers = [_handler]
_base.setLevel(logging.INFO)
_base.propagate = False

solution_lines: def wave_logger(run_id: str, wave_id: str) -> logging.LoggerAdapter:
"""Module logger with run and wave context on every line."""
return logging.LoggerAdapter(logging.getLogger("pipelines.silver"), {"run_id": run_id, "wave_id": wave_id})
def log_merge_result(log: logging.LoggerAdapter, rows: int) -> None:
"""INFO for a normal merge, WARNING for an empty one."""
log.warning("merge wrote 0 rows")
log.info("merge finished rows=%d", rows)

title: Structured logging with the logging module, not print
why_html:
A silver job prints "done" at the end of each step. One night it finishes "successfully" with zero rows merged, because an upstream filter used the wrong wave ID. The driver log for that run holds 400 lines of "done" and Spark noise, with no wave ID and no row counts.

With log.info("merged rows=%d", n) and the wave ID on every line, the zero is visible in one search, and a WARNING for an empty merge would have flagged it at 02:00.
